https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8e.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Anthrax mainly affects grazing animals and can lead to sudden death (file photo) By Basillioh Rukanga Published 9 hours ago Authorities in Zambia have warned people not to eat meat from wildlife after dozens of wild animals, including hippos, elephants, buffalo and a crocodile died following an anthrax outbreak. A disaster management agency official said over the weekend that 12 people had been infected with the disease after consuming dead wildlife in the Munyamadzi River area. The official urged the public not to consume meat from animals that die naturally or from unknown causes, while urging the public to report any such cases. Authorities have also called for hunting in the affected area to be suspended until the extent of the disease and associated risks are established. Officials have not yet ascertained the full geographical extent of the latest outbreak, with surveillance and laboratory investigations ongoing. Anthrax is endemic to Zambia but human deaths are not common. In 2023, the country experienced what was described as an "unprecedented outbreak", which killed four people and spread to nine out of 10 provinces. Another large-scale outbreak was reported in 2011, with more than 500 cases, when five people died after consuming meat from infected hippos. In the latest outbreak in the Munyamadzi Game Management Area, in Muchinga province, Zambia's Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit said 46 hippos, eight elephants, five buffaloes and one crocodile had died since July. "The sad story about the deaths of this wildlife is that the carcasses ended up being eaten by the local people - that's what they depend on for their food," said the unit's national coordinator Norman Chipakupaku. No human deaths have been reported, and the 12 infected people are currently receiving treatment. Anthrax is caused by a bacteria called Bacillus anthracis, which largely survives as spores that hide away in soil for years before entering an animal through inhalation or a cut or wound. It mainly affects grazing animals and can lead to sudden death. It can be transmitted from animals to humans through contact with contaminated animal products. Zambians have been urged not to consume, sell, distribute or handle meat from animals that have died suddenly or from suspected anthrax. The public has also been advised against handling wild animals. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: După ce la sfârșitul săptămânii trecute reactorul 1 de la Centrala Nucleară de la Cernavodă a fost reconectat la Sistemul Energetic Național, după mai bine de trei luni de oprire, luni a fost inițiată secvența de pornire a unității 2 a centralei. Potrivit Ministerului Energiei, reactorul va fi pus în funcțiune marți. Conform datelor Transelectrica, peste 3% din producția totală de energie din acest moment provine de la Centrala de la Cernavodă. Cele două reactoare de la Cernavodă, atunci când sunt ambele în funcțiune, asigură aproximativ 20% din necesarul național de electricitate. Premierul Luca Niculescu și ministrul Energiei, Dumitru Chisăliţă, au fost sâmbătă la Centrala Nuclearoelectrică de la Cernavodă, la o zi după ce unitatea 1 a fost resincronizată la Sistemul Energetic Național, la trei luni de când fusese oprită. https://www.witn.com/2026/10/27/duplin-c.text: Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google DUPLIN COUNTY, N.C. (WITN) - With one week until the midterms, the race for Duplin County sheriff is heating up between Eric Southerland and write-in candidate Charles “Chuck” Weaver. Southerland, the former Warsaw police chief, began his campaign back in 2024. Weaver announced as a write-in candidate earlier this year. The matchup was set after incumbent Stratton Stokes lost in the primaries earlier this year. He announced his resignation in June and named Weaver chief deputy. Soon after, Weaver announced his plans to run as a write-in. Weaver said Tuesday he waited because he was not going to run against his boss. Since announcing in July, he’s been campaigning hard. “It’s been a short amount of time for me; I made my announcement back in July,” Weaver said. “It’s pretty much been four months of really hitting the ground and running pretty hard. Me, along with the support of my campaign crowd, also helping me and pushing me.” Southerland served as Warsaw police chief until retiring in 2020, then began teaching at James Sprunt Community College. He says Duplin County needs change within the sheriff’s office. “Establishing good, solid command structure and clear guidelines and expectations for each men and woman that works for the sheriff’s office,” Southerland said. He says that change starts in the community. “We’re going to change the culture and mindset,” Southerland said. “We’re going to start working in our communities, getting involved and building those relationships that we’ve lost over the years.” Southerland previously told WITN in March that major staffing changes would be coming to the department. Weaver has worked under four sheriffs in Duplin County and says he learned good and bad things from all of them. “My plan is to keep working hard for the citizens of Duplin County, providing security and safety for the community and schools, and enhance on the sheriff’s office, and just making it better for the citizens of Duplin County,” Weaver said. Both candidates have been visiting early voting sites and meeting with residents ahead of Nov. 3. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved. https://www.justsecurity.org/164111/earl.text: Early Edition: November 11, 2026 By Ammanuel Desta Published on November 11, 2026 Listen to Article Sign up to receive the Early Edition in your inbox here . A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news: IRAN WAR U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio yesterday said that the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign against Iran was effective enough that “there’s really no need for major combat operations any longer.” Rubio added that the United States might still respond with force if Iran “crosses certain red lines.” Michael Crowley reports for the New York Times . IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS Iran’s Foreign Ministry today announced the country has designated Argentina’s navy and air force as “terrorist organizations.” The move is reciprocal, and follows Argentina’s April designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards as a terrorist entity. Elwely Elwelly reports for Reuters . Iranian Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei today told Lebanese TV that Iran will not allow even a single particle of enriched nuclear material to leave Iran, and that there will be consequences for any new U.S. strikes. Rezaei said “any new U.S. attacks will also be met with targeting U.S. bases far away.” Elwely Elwelly and Jana Choukeir report for Reuters . U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently moved from his home onto a military base amid Iranian threats against his life, sources told the New York Times . The sources said U.S. officials in recent weeks concluded that Iranian plotting against current and former U.S. officials had reached a more advanced stage, based in part on intelligence about threats to Bessent. The severity of the threats to him is unclear. Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan report. The U.S. Justice Department yesterday announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the United States and Europe. The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently “orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom.” Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the Royal Air Force Fairford incident. Jack Burgess reports for BBC News . ISRAEL-HAMAS WAR Israeli forces yesterday killed at least seven people, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in Gaza, according to local health officials. Medics said the father and son were killed in an airstrike that hit the roof of a displacement shelter in the Zeitoun neighborhood in Gaza City, and health officials said a third person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near a school in Gaza City’s Daraj neighborhood. The Israeli military said it struck militants in both areas. Later strikes in Gaza city killed three more people, while Israeli gunfire killed a man in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis. The IDF did not comment on these incidents. Nidal al-Mughrabi reports for Reuters . RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy yesterday said the first day of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States in Abu Dhabi were “constructive and quite substantive.” Zelenskyy did not attend the meeting himself, and senior officials from Ukraine and Russia were secretive after the four-hour-long discussions. Rubio also said the meeting had been “very productive.” Laura Gozzi and Abdujalil Abdurasulov report for BBC News . Officials at the trilateral talks today said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war as the two-day talks come to a close. U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner said “one of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” Head of the Russian delegation Vladimir Medinsky confirmed the planned exchange. Bassam Hatoum reports for AP News . NATO scrambled jets overnight after at least four drones strayed into the airspace of the Baltic states during Ukrainian strikes on Russia, officials said today. The drones triggered brief alerts to citizens of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to seek shelter. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius described the ordeal as a “difficult night” and confirmed there were no reports of injuries. Andrius Sytas and JekaterĪna Golubkova report for Reuters . NATO allies are considering the biggest overhaul of their military planning in at least two decades to prioritize fighting Russia over providing spare troops for places like Iraq and Afghanistan, four NATO diplomats briefed on the draft planning document told POLITICO . The sources said allies would no longer be expected to provide enough forces to fight a major European war and conduct several smaller crisis-management missions at the same time, but rather enough troops for one scenario or the other. Victor Jack reports. OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS Russia’s Federal Security Service today said it had arrested two people it described as agents of the Polish secret service for gathering information on military facilities in Russia’s western Kaliningrad region, Interfax reports. Interfax also cited the FSB as stating it had warned seven Polish citizens and three Russian nationals over what it said were their contacts with the Polish security services. Reuters reports. A U.K. final court of appeal yesterday struck down a centuries-old gay sex ban in Trinidad and Tobago. Jason Jones in Feb. 2017 filed the case, arguing that “buggery” laws dated back to when Trinidad and Tobago were a U.K. colony are unconstitutional. The judge said “those laws cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedom of the individual.” Dánica Coto reports for AP News . Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara today said at least 300 schools in Italy were evacuated after receiving the same bomb alert message. Valditara told Italian news that the alerts were presumed to be hoaxes, and that the number of schools affected is expected to rise. Alvise Armellini, Giselda Vagnoni, and Giuseppe Fonte report for Reuters . Israeli leader of the Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot yesterday pledged to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies as Israel’s new parliament was sworn in. While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Melanie Lidman reports for AP News . CLIMATE DEVELOPMENTS U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres today told world leaders at the U.N. COP31 conference in Turkey that the slow international response to climate change had placed the world on a path to destruction, and fast action is needed to avert it. Guterres said “the brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction.” Tuvan Gumrukcu and Valerie Volcovici report for Reuters . Australia, Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria, and Vanuatu yesterday endorsed the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels worldwide by 2030. The declaration launched on the second day of the U.N. COP31 conference in Turkey. CEO of the Global Solar Council Sonia Dunlop said “this is the future of affordable energy.” Anton L. Delgado, Sibi Arasu, and Suzan Fraser report for AP News . Climate activist Greta Thunberg yesterday condemned the annual proceedings of COP31 as hypocritical and urged leaders to put people and the planet ahead of profits and power. Thunberg said “it’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo.” Khalil Hamra, Sibi Arasu, and Anton L. Delgado report for AP News . AI DEVELOPMENTS Cybersecurity company CloudSek today published a report that said a hacking group tied to Kazakhstan recently used AI to steal more than 2,000 national security-related documents from Tajikistan. The report said the cyber spies used Hermes, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents, and CloudSek caught them after they inadvertently left a server exposed to the internet. Raphael Satter reports for Reuters . Nvidia yesterday announced that it has hired a former acting U.S. attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim to investigate its CEO Jensen Huang following reports of Jensen’s intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China. Suryatapa Chakraborty reports for The Hill . Chinese university Northwestern Polytechnical last month bought two of Nvidia’s H200 chips for $123,000 despite being on a U.S. export blacklist due to ties to the People’s Liberation Army, according to an Oct. 21 procurement record on the university’s website viewed by Reuters . According to the records, the chips were purchased for the university’s management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia. Eduardo Baptista reports. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Jensen’s relationship with Alice, sources told Axios . On May 14, the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia’s H200 chips, and some export approvals predated the warning. Separately, Rubio in May told Trump aboard Air Force One en route to China that the United States had obtained sensitive intelligence showing Jensen was in a relationship with Alice, sources told the New York Times . Maria Curi and Marc Caputo report; Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes, Ana Swanson, and Tripp Mickle report. U.S. FOREIGN AFFAIRS U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing London yesterday said a U.S. soldier was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. The police said the man, who had been based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023. The suspect was arrested as part of an operation involving U.K.’s MI5 in coordination with the FBI, U.S. and U.K. authorities told the Washington Post . Amy Walker reports for BBC News ; Greg Miller reports. U.S. far-right podcaster Candace Owens on Monday confirmed French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte filed a second set of defamation complaints against her. The Macrons had sued Owens and two of he businesses in Jul. 2025 over what they called a lie-filled “campaign of global humiliation,” including the false claim that Brigitte was born a male. Last month, a Delaware judge ruled that he did not have jurisdiction over Owens, who lives in Tennessee, but that the Macrons could sue Owens’ companies in the state. The new lawsuit concerns Owen’s use of a Brigitte doll they called “grotesque,” and said it was used by Owens as a “prop to ridicule her appearance.” Inti Landauro and Elizabeth Pineau report for Reuters . The federal government in the first nine months of this year received more than $12 billion in revenue from Venezuela’s natural resource exports, according to a confidential report by the global financial services firm KPMG reviewed by the New York Times . The vast majority of the funds were distributed back to Venezuela soon after they were received, but it is unclear if the money stayed in the country or who the ultimate recipients were. Tyler Pager and Anatoly Kurmanaev report. State Department officials quietly raised objections to El Salvador’s gang-fighting efforts in Haiti, even as Trump offered his full support, sources told Axios . El Salvador on Monday issued a formal rebuke that questioned the “credibility” of the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires to Haiti David Howell, after Howell complained in a text message to Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé that El Salvador wasn’t “coordinating” with the U.N.-backed Gang Suppression Force. A U.S. official said “there is a class of bureaucrats who don’t want to see the change in the Western Hemisphere that POTUS wants.” Marc Caputo reports. U.S. IMMIGRATION DEVELOPMENTS A deportation flight from Arizona to Pakistan carrying Iranians bound for Iran yesterday turned around midair and landed back in Arizona, a legal defense group and a flight-tracking monitor told the New York Times . The flight turned around after Pakistan abruptly declined to accept them, according to a relative of a detainee who said an Iranian official shared that information, and added that the Iranian detainees were returned to the Arizona immigration detention facility. Pranav Baskar, Hamed Aleaziz, Salman Masood, and Zach Montague report. At least 19 ICE recruits named in the recent Department of Homeland Security hack were hired despite red flags, according to a background check using public records conducted by the Washington Post . The Trump administration’s accelerated recruitment drive for its immigration agenda resulted in traditional background checks being ignored. At least two of these hires in recent months have been involved in shootings, including one which resulted in the death of a Colombian father. Some of the officers have been fired after the red flags initially missed were discovered. Ted Hesson, Joyce Sohyun Lee, Razzan Nakhlawi, Maria Sacchetti, and Aaron Schaffer report. David Brouillette, the ICE officer who fatally shot a Colombian migrant in Maine this summer, has a deep-seated anti-immigrant hostility, especially against Colombians, according to copies of emails he sent to his family shared with the New York Times . Brouillette, a former U.S. Army sergeant, wrote disparagingly to his sister and their relatives about a Colombian man with whom his sister had two children. The email said “He can take his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries.” Katie Benner and Alexandra Berzon report. A federal judge on Monday ordered the release of UC Berkeley student and asylum seeker Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez. The Colombian national was detained at San Francisco International Airport on Oct. 30. Albornoz Hernandez’s attorneys argued that her detention violated the U.S. constitution because she was deprived of her liberty without an opportunity to challenge it in court, while the DHS said Albornoz Hernandez was deportable because she had overstayed a visa in 2023, her work authorization and pending asylum application did not confer legal status, and that “being in detention is a choice” because immigrants have the opportunity to self deport. The judge said “due process forbids the government from detaining the noncitizen unless they are first provided with adequate notice and pre-deprivation hearing before a neutral arbiter.” Felicia Mello reports for AP News . The DOJ saw a green card application by the former bodyguard of House Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN), Abdullahi Mohamed, as an opportunity to gather evidence against Omar, sources told the New York Times . Federal prosecutors earlier this year filed a felony charge against Mohamed for lying to a government official under oath. Mohamed’s lawyer said that prosecutors spent months trying to turn the bodyguard into an informant to bolster their case against Omar. Ernesto Londoño and Abdi Latif Dahir report. U.S. MIDTERM DEVELOPMENTS An Alaska state judge yesterday said he expects to issue a swift decision in a lawsuit filed by the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, which is seeking a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected. Peltola’s campaign also said it wants to know the reasons for the rejections and said its intent is to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. Attorneys for the state say the information requested would violate voter privacy. Becky Bohrer reports for AP News .
